one_liner: Header-only C++ FuzzyWuzzy-style string similarity scorers on bit-parallel LCS/Levenshtein; its Python package runs 13-28x more pairs/s than FuzzyWuzzy.
what_it_does: A C++ reimplementation and extension of FuzzyWuzzy's scorers (fuzz::ratio, partial_ratio, token_sort_ratio, token_set_ratio, their partial variants, QRatio, WRatio) plus raw string metrics (Levenshtein, Damerau-Levenshtein, OSA, Indel, LCSseq, Hamming, Jaro, Jaro-Winkler, Prefix, Postfix) with distance, similarity, normalized and editops/opcodes variants over any iterator range. Every scorer comes as a free function and as a Cached* class that preprocesses one query once and then scores it against many choices; x86 builds also get experimental Multi* classes that score many short queries at once. It is not a drop-in for the Python API: C++ has no process.extract/extractOne/cdist and no default_process string normalizer, so the README tells you to write the candidate loop (and any lowercasing or punctuation stripping) yourself.
how_it_is_fast: ratio is an Indel (LCS-based) similarity computed with Hyyro's bit-parallel LCS, and Levenshtein uses the Hyyro 2003 bit-vector recurrence (Myers-style), 64 characters per machine word, blocked for longer strings and limited to an Ukkonen band when a score_cutoff is given; when only a few edits are allowed it switches to the mbleven model enumeration, and common prefixes and suffixes are stripped first. Cached* scorers build the per-character bitmask table once per query (a 256-entry array for 8-bit characters, a 128-slot open-addressing hashmap otherwise). The experimental Multi* scorers (MultiRatio, MultiTokenSortRatio, MultiQRatio, MultiIndel, MultiLCSseq, MultiLevenshtein, MultiJaro) pack many queries into one SSE2/AVX2 register (8-bit lanes for queries up to 8 characters, i.e. 32 per 256-bit vector; 16, 32 and 64-bit lanes up to 64 characters) and advance the bit-parallel recurrence for all of them per choice. score_cutoff lets scorers exit early, and partial_ratio skips alignment windows whose best possible score is below the current best.
when_to_use: Scoring short strings (names, product titles, addresses, OCR tokens up to about 64 characters) against thousands to millions of candidates in C++, with one Cached* scorer per query and a score_cutoff to prune.

Porting Python code that used FuzzyWuzzy, thefuzz or the RapidFuzz package to C++: the Python package compiles this exact library from its extern/rapidfuzz-cpp submodule, so scores match the Python package.
You need FuzzyWuzzy-style scoring under MIT instead of FuzzyWuzzy's GPL.
Batch scoring on x86-64 where queries are at most 64 characters and you can compile with -mavx2 (or at least SSE2): the experimental Multi* classes give the cdist-style batched speedup.
Edit-distance building blocks for generic sequences (wide strings, code points, integer token ids) that also need editops/opcodes alignments.
when_not_to_use: Searching a large corpus: there is no index, so every query is a linear scan over all candidates; put an inverted index, n-gram or BK-tree prefilter in front for large collections.

Long strings: the SIMD multi-string path only covers queries up to 64 characters (longer ones fall back to one scorer per query), and partial_ratio cost grows with needle length times haystack windows. For batched plain Levenshtein on ~100-byte strings, StringZilla's README (competitor-run, one core) shows 15,680 MCUPS for its C kernel vs 4,970 for rapidfuzz.process.cdist on a Sapphire Rapids Xeon (3.2x, derived from page data) and 22,844 vs 18,370 on an Apple M5 Pro.

Unicode-aware matching out of the box: the C++ library has no case folding or normalization and compares the elements it is given, so a UTF-8 std::string is compared byte by byte; decode to char32_t and preprocess yourself.
Non-x86 SIMD: the SIMD layer is selected at compile time from __AVX2__ or __SSE2__ only, so aarch64 and other targets get the scalar bit-parallel code and no Multi* classes.

You need bit-identical FuzzyWuzzy output: partial_ratio searches for the optimal alignment where FuzzyWuzzy used a SequenceMatcher matching-block heuristic, and FuzzyWuzzy's ratio without python-Levenshtein is difflib's Ratcliff-Obershelp score, not Indel.

integration.form: header-only (CMake INTERFACE target rapidfuzz::rapidfuzz; a single-file extras/rapidfuzz_amalgamated.hpp also exists but is stale)
integration.dependencies: none (Catch2 only for RAPIDFUZZ_BUILD_TESTING, Google Benchmark only for RAPIDFUZZ_BUILD_BENCHMARKS, both off by default)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 since 3.3.0 (2025-01-18; earlier releases needed C++17); CMake 3.5+; 3.3.2 fixed builds on old MSVC versions without proper if constexpr
integration.platforms: any C++11 target for the scalar bit-parallel code; SIMD Multi* scorers only on x86/x86-64 with SSE2, or AVX2 when the translation unit is compiled with AVX2 enabled (compile-time choice, no runtime dispatch in the C++ library); a 32-bit SIMD scoring bug was fixed in 3.1.1
integration.thread_safety: not documented; scorer similarity() methods are const and the README's OpenMP example shares one CachedRatio across threads
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same scorer names and FuzzyWuzzy-compatible scores, but it replaces a Python library with a C++ one; no extract/extractOne/cdist and no full_process/default_process cleaning in C++, and partial_ratio (optimal alignment) and ratio (Indel, not difflib) can differ from FuzzyWuzzy

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the 258x-717x cdist figures: the chart's strings are 8 characters, exactly the narrowest SIMD lane width, so RapidFuzz's cdist packs 32 queries (256/8) per AVX2 batch, and the batched Multi* path exists only for ratio, token_sort_ratio and QRatio, the three biggest bars (258x, 717x, 622x); the README text says length 10, which would give 16 per batch. In the script as it ran for the chart (commit 69fc902, 2022-10-02) RapidFuzz's cdist applied default_process once per string while FuzzyWuzzy's token_*, QRatio and WRatio scorers ran their own full_process inside each of the 1,000,000 timed calls, so preprocessing was hoisted only on the RapidFuzz side.

Neither chart can be reproduced as published: commit 6925381 (2023-04-12, 'fix some linter warnings') made benchmark_cdist.py call processor(x) where processor is the bool True, which raises TypeError for 6 of the 8 scorers; RapidFuzz 3.0.0 (2023-04-16) removed boolean processors and made processor=None the default, so benchmark_scorer.py rerun today compares unpreprocessed RapidFuzz scorers with FuzzyWuzzy's per-call full_process; bench/requirements.txt lists thefuzz (built on rapidfuzz itself since 0.20.0) rather than fuzzywuzzy, whose last release is 0.18.0 from 2020.

Both charts use only equal-length strings and predate the 1.10.2 fix (2022-12-01) that made partial_ratio symmetric when len(s1) == len(s2): current code runs a second, reversed pass in that case unless the first score is 100, so today's partial_ratio and partial_token_* do up to twice the work that was measured. The cdist chart also ran SIMD code added the same day (rapidfuzz-cpp 1.8.0) before fixes for undefined behavior (1.10.2) and broken SSE2 support (1.10.1).

Pin a recent release and use the rapidfuzz/ headers, not extras/rapidfuzz_amalgamated.hpp: the amalgamated file's banner still says 'RapidFuzz v1.0.2, Generated 2025-02-11' and it keeps the WRatio 'len_ratio < 8.0' branch that 3.3.3 fixed to '<= 8.0'; 3.0.5 fixed editops miscounts and crashes and 3.3.4 (2026-08-29) an out-of-bounds access in Editops::remove_subsequence. API reference docs are effectively absent (issue #130: the Doxygen output is empty).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued siblings scores string similarity: Tantivy, SeekStorm, PISA, IResearch, Manticore and Infinity rank documents from an inverted index, and ugrep, ngi, trigrep and frg find literal or regex matches in files. Pick RapidFuzz when you already have a candidate list and need an edit-distance score per pair, or to rerank the top hits such an engine returns.
verified_claims_summary: First-party charts from the Python package that compiles this library: per-pair calls from a Python list comprehension over 100 x 10,000 random 10-character alphanumeric strings ran 12.9x (ratio) to 28.3x (QRatio) more pairs per second than FuzzyWuzzy, and one single-threaded cdist call on 8-character strings ran 27x to 717x more than a Python double loop over FuzzyWuzzy; each is a single timeit run with no CPU, compiler, flags, Python or FuzzyWuzzy version stated and no word on whether python-Levenshtein was installed, and the space-free strings make every token scorer a single-token case. No C++-to-C++ comparison exists; the C++ repo's Google Benchmark files (built with -march=native) time only RapidFuzz itself.
status_note: Actively maintained (rapidfuzz-cpp 3.3.4 on 2026-08-29, Python package 3.14.6 on 2026-08-30), MIT and header-only so easy to vendor, but the headline numbers are Python-level, their scripts no longer run, and the cdist ratios hinge on 8-character strings hitting the 32-lane AVX2 path, so measure C++ speed with your own harness.
